newsitem.title: USA: U.S. power plants to make bigger cuts in pollution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. power plants to make bigger cuts in pollution.

text.p: Electric power plants will have to reduce emissions of acid-rain producing nitrogen oxide by nearly 900,000 tons annually starting in 2000, the Environmental Protection Agency announced Friday.
Electric power plants produce one-third of nitrogen oxide (NOx) air pollution, which may cause lung damage and respiratory illness, and contribute to smog and acid rain, the EPA said in a statement.
With the new rule, the second stage of the Clean Air Act's acid rain programme, they must cut NOx emissions by another 15 percent from utilities' current levels.
The rule sets NOx emissions limits for most of the 1,090 coal-fired power plants in the nation that can generate more than 25 megawatts.
It revises earlier standards for about 600 boilers, and sets new emission standards for about 145 others.

The EPA estimated 85 to 90 percent of plants affected by this rule would be able to meet the standard with available technologies. Utilities will pay an estimated $200 million annually to comply, it said.
But the Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities, said that estimate was low.
"It will be far more than $200 million," Bob Beck, the EEI's vice president for environmental affairs, said.

He said utilities would have to use expensive selective catalytic reduction technology on some boilers, and the new rule would force some utilities that just installed pollution control devices on boilers to install new devices to meet the higher standards.
Utilities likely will challenge the new rule in court, Beck said.
The EPA in its statement also encouraged states to adopt emissions trading programmes as an alternative to meeting emissions limits prescribed for each utility boiler.

Those programmes allow utilities that exceed emission reductions at one plant to have excess emissions at another. But the final result must be lower NOx emissions than would have resulted from meeting plant-by-plant limits.
